newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices rebound, oil drops sharply.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices rebound, oil drops sharply.

text.p: Coffee prices rose on Tuesday to end a bout of profit-taking by traders from 20-year highs as attention returned to tight supplies and concerns about wintry weather in Brazil's coffee region this month.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery closed 10.25 cents a pound higher at 264.20 cents.
Since peaking at 318.00 cents a pound last Thursday -- the highest coffee price since June 1977 -- the July contract had tumbled nearly 70 cents the last two trading sessions.
"It came down two days hard," said Stephen Smith, president of South Futures. "You could look at it as a golden opportunity to buy this market.

"This is still a no-coffee situation, and there's no coffee coming in with all the Central Americans at the end of their crop cycle," Smith said. "We've got cold weather (in Brazil) in the background, and who wants to be short?"
Low coffee stockpiles in consuming and producing countries should keep prices well supported, with any threat of frost in top grower Brazil sparking a rally.
"People were discounting the weather situation this morning and the market came under pressure," Prudential Securities analyst Arthur Stevenson said.
But the July contract's ability to hold above Monday's low of 247.50 cents was seen as a buy signal by traders who follow price charts and sparked renewed buying.
"At the moment it is a chart-type market waiting for some new fundamentals," Stevenson said.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices closed lower in anticipation of increases in oil and product stocks and production in weekly data from the American Petroleum Institute on Tuesday afternoon.

Crude oil for July delivery fell 65 cents a barrel to close at $20.33, with July unleaded gasoline ending down 1.55 cents a gallon at 61.44 cents and July heating oil down 1.70 cents a gallon at 54.62 cents.

After the close of trading, the API reported rises in stocks of crude oil and gasoline in the United States in the week ended May 30, as well as record gasoline output at the start of the summer vacation driving season.

"They look pretty bearish," said Thomas Blakeslee, a Cargill Investors Services trader, referring to the API data. "Clearly, operations are up pretty sharply here and we're seeing very high supply figures."

Gasoline production hit a record 8.195 million barrels per day last week. Even with the nation's refineries running at a whopping 98.4 percent of capacity, crude oil stocks rose another 8.4 million barrels on the week as imports remained high.
The API reported crude stocks up at 324 million barrels, nearly 14 million barrels above the year-earlier level.
At the New York Cotton Exchange, orange juice prices edged higher on talk of a possible threat to Florida citrus groves from the Mediterranean fruit fly, a dreaded pest.
Frozen concentrated orange juice for July delivery closed 0.45 cent a pound higher at 77.50 cents.
Analysts and juice processors said about 40 "medflies" had been discovered in residential areas in Hillsborough County, near Tampa in Florida, and some larvae were found in fruit.

But spraying to eradicate the flies was slated to start later this week, said Lisa Backman of Florida Citrus Mutual, a growers organization. "We are quite confident they will be successful in eradicating the fly," Backman said.

Platinum group metals on the New York Mercantile Exchange continued to rise, shrugging off indications that Russian exports would resume soon. Russian exports have been suspended since last December, forcing a drawdown of world inventories.
But Japanese trade houses are now in talks with Russian officials over a resumption of exports.
July platinum ended up $3.00 at $401.70 an ounce and September palladium up $5.35 at $169.65 an ounce, with current tight supplies on world markets overcoming the Russian news.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for July delivery closed up 1-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.62 on forecasts for continued cool wet weather in the eastern Midwest, which could cut soft red winter wheat yield potential.
July soybeans plummeted to close 15-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $8.60 on talk that U.S. processors of soybeans may step up imports of South American beans due to high prices here.
"The explanation for the sell-off in July is the continued concern about imports coming from Brazil," said Anne Frick, oilseeds analyst with Prudential Securities.
